t: Aim and plan of the session
n: In this session we will learn to analyse tropane, quinoline and opium alkaloids. Topic: detection of the alkaloids atropine, scopolamine, quinine and papaverine in an extract, and the use of gel chromatography. Aim: to teach the use, poisoning cases, metabolism, isolation and analytical methods of alkaloids containing a tropane derivative. Plan: tropane derivatives, that is atropine, hyoscyamine and scopolamine, and the quinoline derivative quinine, their toxicological significance and methods of analysis.

Expected outcomes. Students become familiar with methods of isolating tropane and quinoline derivatives, their toxicological significance, and qualitative and quantitative analysis. The shape of microcrystals is drawn, and colour and fluorescence reactions are performed. For atropine, scopolamine, quinine and papaverine, TLC and UV spectral data are compared.

Equipment and apparatus. Required items: test tubes, separating funnels, reagents and visual aids. The session is held in a room equipped with special laboratory facilities. For the Vitali-Morin reaction a porcelain dish and a water bath are needed. For microcrystalloscopy a microscope slide, a humid chamber and a microscope are used. To observe quinine fluorescence, an ultraviolet light source is required.

List of reagents. For atropine and scopolamine: concentrated HNO3, acetone, an alcoholic solution of sodium hydroxide, 1% Reinecke salt, picric acid and Dragendorff reagent. For scopolamine, gold bromide acid is also needed, that is a mixture of 5% gold bromide acid, concentrated HCl and acetone in equal proportions, as well as a KBr crystal. For quinine: dilute H2SO4, bromine water, ammonia and K3[Fe(CN)6]. For papaverine: 10% cadmium chloride, iodine solution and Marquis reagent.

Safety and preparation. For the laboratory work the student brings rubber gloves, a wipe and a face mask. The examination is carried out in rooms with ventilation and a fume cupboard, which are locked and sealed when the work is finished. Objects from infected persons, that is those with tuberculosis, hepatitis or AIDS, arrive in a special container and are noted in the documents.

t: Tropane, quinoline and opium alkaloids: classification
n: Classification of alkaloids. Plan of the session: tropane derivatives, that is atropine, hyoscyamine and scopolamine, and the quinoline derivative quinine. Atropine is obtained from the belladonna plant, scopolamine from henbane. Quinine is obtained from cinchona bark. Papaverine occurs in opium and has no narcotic action. Thus today's alkaloids fall into three groups: tropane derivatives, a quinoline derivative and an opium alkaloid.

Structure and properties of atropine. Atropine is an ester formed from tropine alcohol and tropic acid, and is isolated from the belladonna plant. Hyoscyamine is an isomer of atropine, differing only in that it rotates polarised light to the left. In base form atropine dissolves well in organic solvents and poorly in water. Its sulphate salt dissolves well in water. Atropine is isolated by extraction with organic solvents from an alkaline medium.

Toxicological significance of atropine. In poisoning, the nervous system is first excited: convulsions, involuntary speech and laughter are observed. Then the endings of the parasympathetic nerves are paralysed and the pupil dilates. Dryness and reddening of the nose and skin are noted. When death occurs, the pathological examination is not characteristic. 50% of atropine is excreted unchanged in the urine, and the rest breaks down into tropic acid and tropine. Data on its persistence in the body vary: it breaks down quickly, or persists for 3 weeks, even up to 2 years.

t: Atropine and scopolamine: structure and source
n: Let us compare atropine and scopolamine. Atropine is an ester of tropine alcohol and tropic acid, while scopolamine is an ester of scopine and tropic acid. Atropine is obtained from belladonna, scopolamine from henbane. Atropine is isolated with organic solvents from an alkaline medium, and scopolamine is extracted at pH=8-10. In medicine atropine is used as the sulphate, and scopolamine as the bromide.

Procedure for the Vitali-Morin reaction. To 3-4 drops of the chloroform residue, 1 ml of concentrated HNO3 is added and evaporated on a water bath until the acid has gone. The residue is cooled. To the cooled yellow residue, 2-3 drops of acetone are added from one side and 2-3 drops of alcoholic alkali from the other. As a result a rapidly fading violet colour forms.

The essence and interpretation of the Vitali-Morin reaction. When atropine is heated with concentrated HNO3, it breaks down into tropic acid and tropine, and the yellow nitro derivative gives a violet compound in alkali. However, the reaction is not characteristic of atropine: nitrogenous compounds containing a benzene ring, that is hyoscyamine, scopolamine, strychnine and apomorphine, also give it. Dicaine also gives the Vitali-Morin reaction. If the reaction is negative, atropine is absent. If it is positive, additional confirmatory reactions are needed.

Scheme of the Vitali-Morin reaction. When atropine is heated with concentrated HNO3, it breaks down into tropic acid and tropine, and a yellow nitro derivative forms. Under the action of alkali the nitro derivative gives a violet-coloured compound. Reagents: atropine residue, concentrated HNO3, acetone and alcoholic NaOH. The reaction is carried out on a water bath until the acid has gone. When atropine is present, a rapidly fading violet colour forms.

Microcrystals of atropine. Reaction with Reinecke salt: 1 drop of 0.1 M HCl and 2 drops of fresh 1% Reinecke salt are added, and after 15-20 minutes pale pink rhombic crystals form. With a saturated aqueous solution of picric acid, kept for 15-20 minutes in a humid chamber, yellow plate-shaped crystals appear. We draw the shape of the crystals in the work notebook.

Atropine: p-dimethylaminobenzaldehyde and the pharmacological test. To the residue obtained from the alkaline medium, 3-5 drops of a 0.5% solution of p-DMABA in concentrated H2SO4 are added. It is heated for 5-10 minutes on a boiling water bath. If atropine is present, a red colour forms. In the pharmacological test, dilation of the pupil is observed.

Sequence of detection of atropine. First the general precipitating reagents are used, then the Vitali-Morin reaction. For confirmation, crystals with Reinecke salt and picric acid, TLC and the UV spectrum are used. In TLC Rf=0.26, UV maxima at 252, 258, 264 nm. The final stage is the pharmacological test, in which the pupils of experimental animals dilate.

Main indicators of atropine. Of the atropine that has entered the body, 50% is excreted unchanged in the urine. In TLC in the chloroform-acetone-diethylamine system, in the ratio 50:30:2, Rf=0.26. UV maxima at 252, 258, 264 nm. Microcrystalline reactions are kept in a humid chamber for 15-20 minutes, and with p-DMABA the mixture is heated on a water bath for 5-10 minutes.

About scopolamine. Scopolamine occurs in henbane; it is an ester composed of scopine and tropic acid. In medicine it is used as the bromide; the Aeron tablet is part of antiemetic and sedative drugs. It is isolated with organic solvents from an alkaline medium at pH=8-10. Like atropine, it dilates the pupil, relaxes the muscles of mucous membranes and reduces glandular secretion.

Microcrystalline reactions of scopolamine. With Reinecke salt, dendrite-shaped light brown, yellow and reddish crystals form. With Dragendorff reagent, brown short needle-like crystals appear. With gold bromide acid reagent and a KBr crystal, yellow-reddish toothed dendrites form. The crystal shape differs with each reagent, so we will examine all three.

t: Atropine and scopolamine: TLC and UV spectrum
n: Atropine and scopolamine: TLC and UV spectrum. The TLC system is chloroform-acetone-diethylamine, in the ratio 50:30:2. In this system atropine gives Rf=0.26 and scopolamine Rf=0.44. In a solution in 0.1 M H2SO4, atropine has maxima at 252, 258, 264 nm, and scopolamine at 251, 257, 263 nm. As can be seen, the UV maxima are very close to each other, while the Rf values differ clearly.

t: Scopolamine: reaction with gold bromide acid
n: Detection of scopolamine with gold bromide acid. To the residue on a microscope slide, 1 drop of 0.1 M HCl is added. Then the reagent, a mixture of 5% gold bromide acid, concentrated HCl and acetone in equal proportions, is added. A KBr crystal is dropped onto the reagent. If scopolamine is present, yellow-reddish crystals in the form of toothed dendrites form.

General information about quinine. Quinine is a derivative of quinoline and quinuclidine, obtained from cinchona bark and synthesised in 1944. In base form it is a bitter-tasting crystal; poorly soluble in water, well soluble in organic solvents. In an alkaline medium, at pH=9-10, it passes into the organic layer. In medicine it is used as the chloride, dihydrochloride and sulphate salts, as an antimalarial and in obstetrics. In metabolism 2-hydroxyquinine, dihydroxyquinine and others are formed, which are excreted in the urine.

Quinine: metabolism and excretion. In the body quinine is metabolised through oxidation of the quinoline and quinuclidine nuclei. This forms 2-hydroxyquinine, dihydroxyquinine and other metabolites. The metabolites and partly unbound quinine are excreted from the body in the urine.

The fluorescence reaction of quinine. The residue is dissolved in 5 ml of dilute H2SO4 and transferred to a test tube. If the solution is viewed in ultraviolet light, a blue shimmer, that is fluorescence, is seen. When ammonia is added, at pH=9, the blue colour disappears and violet fluorescence appears.

Quinine: the thalleioquin reaction. To the residue, 1 ml of water is added, then bromine water until a yellow colour forms, and quickly 3-5 drops of ammonia. The solution turns blue. The colour depends on the medium: in a neutral medium it is green, in an acidic medium red-violet.

Quinine: the erythroquin reaction. After 4 ml of the chloroform solution has been evaporated, 1 ml of water is added to the residue and it is transferred to a test tube. If K3[Fe(CN)6], bromine water and ammonia solution are added to the solution, a red-violet colour forms. This colour is the result of the erythroquin reaction.

Scheme of the thalleioquin reaction. To the chloroform residue in a porcelain dish, 1 ml of water, bromine water and 3-5 drops of ammonia are added. Bromine water is added dropwise until a yellow colour forms, and ammonia is added quickly. When quinine is present, the solution turns blue, in a neutral medium green, in an acidic medium red-violet.

Distinguishing thalleioquin from erythroquin. For thalleioquin, bromine water and ammonia are used, and the result is a blue colour. For erythroquin, K3[Fe(CN)6], bromine water and ammonia are used; ammonia makes the medium alkaline, and the result is a red-violet colour. The thalleioquin reaction is interfered with by excess bromine, antipyrine and amidopyrine. Therefore bromine water must be added carefully, drop by drop.

Quinine: TLC and UV spectrum. The TLC system is ether-acetone-25% NH4OH, in the ratio 40:20:2. Detection is by fluorescence or with Dragendorff reagent, Rf=0.39. In the UV spectrum quinine in alcohol has maxima at 236, 278, 332 nm, and in 0.1 M H2SO4 at 250, 316, 346 nm. That is, when the medium changes, the maxima change as well.

Detection of quinine in urine. 2 ml of urine is brought to pH=10 with 10% ammonia and shaken for 5 minutes with 4 ml of chloroform or ether. The organic layer is separated and shaken with 3 ml of 10% H2SO4. If light blue fluorescence is seen in ultraviolet light, this indicates the presence of quinine.

About papaverine. Papaverine occurs in opium at about 0.1-1.5%, and is also synthesised. The base is a colourless crystal, rhombic or needle-shaped, with a melting point of 147 °C. Because it is a weak base, it passes into chloroform even under acidic conditions. It is a vasodilator and antispasmodic agent; the maximum dose is 0.1 g; it has no narcotic action. Metabolism is mainly associated with demethylation, and the phenols are excreted in the urine as glucuronides.

Reactions of papaverine. If the residue is dissolved in 0.1 N HCl and 10% cadmium chloride is added dropwise, colourless cubic plates form. Iodine solution gives a red colour, with a sensitivity of 0.1 µg. In the Sobolev reaction with Marquis reagent, methylenebis-papaverine forms; when bromine water and ammonia are added, a stable violet colour appears.

Papaverine: TLC and UV spectrum. The TLC system is chloroform-acetone-diethylamine, in the ratio 50:30:2, with Dragendorff as the developing reagent; Rf=0.75. A solution of papaverine base in 0.1 N HCl has maxima at 250, 284 and 310 nm. These two indicators are used to confirm the authenticity of papaverine.

Methods of detecting papaverine. Papaverine gives a precipitate with alkaloid-precipitating reagents, that is Dragendorff, Bouchardat, Mayer and Sonnenschein. With cadmium chloride, cubic plates form. With iodine solution a red colour forms, and in the Sobolev reaction a violet colour. In TLC Rf=0.75, in the UV spectrum 250, 284, 310 nm.

Main indicators of papaverine. Papaverine occurs in opium at about 0.1-1.5%, with a maximum dose of 0.1 g. The melting point of papaverine base is 147 °C, and that of the hydrochloride 225-226 °C. The sensitivity of the reaction with iodine solution is 0.1 µg of papaverine.

Fundamentals of gel chromatography. In gel chromatography the same solvent is used as the mobile and the stationary phase. Separation depends on molecular size: large molecules are eluted first, then small ones. Gels were first used in 1959 by Porath and Flodin for liquid mixtures. The method is used in column and thin-layer forms.

t: Order of separation in gel chromatography
n: Order of separation in gel chromatography. The mixture is applied to the gel layer. On filtration through the gel, small molecules are absorbed into the pores of the gel and retained. Large molecules move with the solvent between the gel particles. Therefore large molecules are eluted first, then small ones.

t: Types of gels and choice of solvent
n: Types of gels and choice of solvent. Gels are divided into soft, semi-rigid and rigid types. Soft gels include Sephadex and polyacrylamide, which swell in the solvent; gel filtration is used with a soft gel. Styragel is an example of a semi-rigid gel, which swells 1.1-1.8 times. Rigid gels are silica gel and porous glass, whose volume does not change. The solvent must dissolve the mixture, wet the gel surface, and swell a soft gel.

t: Preparing the column in gel chromatography
n: Preparing the column in gel chromatography. If a soft gel is used, the gel must first be soaked and swollen in the solvent taken for the separation. When semi-rigid gels are used, a gel slurry, that is a suspension, is prepared first. For gel chromatography, tubes with an internal diameter of 8-10 mm are used. Increasing the tube diameter to 50 mm raises efficiency.

t: Case: positive result for tropane alkaloids
n: Case: positive result for tropane alkaloids. CASE 21: the biological object gave a positive result for tropane alkaloids in all analyses, yet no poisoning had occurred. "Cadaveric atropine" gives the Vitali-Morin reaction but does not dilate the pupil. For this reason the chemical analysis is supplemented by the pharmacological test.

Photometric methods. Determining the amount of substances by light absorption is called photometry. Colorimetry is based on comparing a coloured solution by eye or with a device. Photocolorimetry uses polychromatic light and the visible part of the spectrum. Spectrophotometry uses monochromatic light in the visible, UV and IR regions.

Review questions. Name the alkaloids containing a tropane derivative; from which plant are atropine and scopolamine obtained, and how do they differ from hyoscyamine? How can atropine and scopolamine be isolated from physical evidence and from liquid materials; what are the signs of poisoning and the metabolites? Explain the Vitali-Morin reaction, the microcrystalline reactions of atropine, the microcrystalloscopic reactions of scopolamine, and their quantification. For quinine and papaverine, state the toxicological significance, isolation, general reactions, fluorescence and colour reactions, and physicochemical methods.

Conclusion and report. Atropine: a rapidly fading violet colour in the Vitali-Morin reaction, Rf=0.26. Scopolamine: toothed dendrites with gold bromide acid, Rf=0.44. Quinine: blue fluorescence, thalleioquin blue, erythroquin red-violet, Rf=0.39. Papaverine: cubic plates with cadmium chloride, red colour with iodine, Rf=0.75. Gel chromatography separates substances by molecular size.
